# Campeyyajātaka (Ja 506)

**ID:** Ja 506
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Campeyyajātaka
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul14.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Campeyyajātaka* (Ja 506) is a canonical Pali birth story set in Jetavana, delivered by the Buddha to lay followers undertaking the fast-day (*uposatha*) vows. The frame story illustrates how ancient sages abandoned even the pleasures of serpentine kingship in order to uphold moral observances [Fausböll 1887]. In the narrative of the past, the Bodhisatta, having admired the majestic radiance of a serpent king during a virtuous human life of almsgiving, is reborn as the nāga king Campeyya [Collins 1998; Fenn 1994]. Distressed by his animal embodiment—which he perceives as an obstacle to spiritual advancement—he leaves his splendid aquatic palace to keep the *uposatha* vows atop an anthill in the human realm [Appleton 2014; Collins 1998; Fenn 1994; Scheible 2011]. When captured, abused, and exploited by a snake-charmer (*ahiguṇḍika*), Campeyya willingly surrenders his body and endures torment rather than breaking his vows through anger [Appleton 2014; Bodhi 2003; Berkwitz 2006]. In the epilogue (*samodhāna*), the snake-charmer is revealed to have been Devadatta, the nāga queen Sumanā is identified as Rāhulamātā, King Uggasena as Sāriputta, and Campeyya as the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1887].

Together with the *Bhūridatta-* (Ja 543) and *Saṅkhapāla-jātaka* (Ja 524), the text forms a notable triad of stories in which the Bodhisatta takes birth as a nāga who practices renunciation and restraint upon an anthill [Appleton 2014; Scheible 2011]. In later canonical and commentarial systematizations—including the *Cariyāpiṭaka* and the *Jātakanidānakathā*—the tale is celebrated as a paramount illustration of the perfection of morality (*sīlapāramī*) [Berkwitz 2006; Gaffney 2003; Scheible 2011]. A critical study of the text alongside the *Saṅkhapālajātaka* was conducted by Thomas Oberlies (1990) [Marciniak 2019].

- [Appleton 2014] Naomi Appleton, Narrating Karma and Rebirth: Buddhist and Jain Multi-life Stories (2014) — Analyzes the Bodhisatta's nāga rebirths, uposatha observance, capture by snake-charmers, and connection to the Mahāvastu.
- [Collins 1998] Steven Collins, Nirvana and other Buddhist felicities (1998) — Details Campeyya's remorse at having taken an animal birth and the English rendering 'Birth Story about Campeyya'.
- [Fenn 1994] Mavis Lillian Fenn, The Concept of Poverty in the Pali Canon (1994) — Discusses Campeyya's previous human life of almsgiving and his aspiration to attain liberation from serpentine form.
- [Bodhi 2003] Bhikkhu Bodhi, The Connected Discourses of the Buddha: A New Translation of the Saṃyutta Nikāya (2000/2003) — Notes the story as the classic exemplar of nāgas upholding uposatha vows even under mortal torment.
- [Berkwitz 2006] Stephen C. Berkwitz, The History of the Buddha's Relic Shrine: A Translation of the Sinhala Thūpavaṃsa (2006) — Identifies the narrative motif of the nāga on an anthill and its classification under the perfection of morality in the Jātakaṭṭhakathā.
- [Fausböll 1887] V. Fausböll, The Jātaka together with its Commentary, Vol. IV (1887) — Supplies opening verses, commentary context, and the concluding identification of past and present characters (samodhāna).
- [Gaffney 2003] Sean D. Gaffney, The Jātakanidānakathā: A Critical Study (2003) — Shows the inclusion of the Campeyya episode under the perfection of morality (sīlapāramī).
- [Marciniak 2019] Katarzyna Marciniak, Mahāvastu: A New Edition, Vol. III (2019) — Bibliographic reference to Thomas Oberlies's 1990 text-critical study of the Campeyya-Jātaka.
- [Scheible 2011] Kristin Scheible, Ph.D. dissertation on the Mahāvaṃsa — Examines the three nāga births of the Bodhisatta and their canonical placement under the sīlapāramī in the Cariyāpiṭaka.
